cases.abstract: ConvNeXt examines how much of hierarchical vision Transformers' performance can be recovered without attention by updating convolutional design and training. We progressively modify ResNet under a fixed modern training recipe, combining depthwise spatial filtering, inverted bottlenecks, larger kernels, and simpler activation and normalization patterns. The resulting network separates spatial and channel mixing while retaining a conventional convolutional hierarchy, without shifted-window attention or relative position biases. Training changes alone raise ResNet-50 ImageNet-1K accuracy from 76.1% to 78.8%, showing that older training recipes account for part of the apparent architectural gap. At 384 x 384 resolution, ConvNeXt-B trained on ImageNet-1K reaches 85.1% accuracy versus Swin-B's 84.5%, with 12.5% higher inference throughput on a V100 GPU. ImageNet-22K pretraining supports further scaling, with ConvNeXt-XL reaching 87.8% after ImageNet-1K fine-tuning. COCO detection and instance segmentation and ADE20K semantic segmentation also yield results comparable to or better than the evaluated Swin counterparts. These evaluations support modernized convolution as a competitive choice for the tested visual recognition tasks, while leaving attention's utility for multimodal and structured-output problems unresolved.
cases.methods: ConvNeXt separates spatial filtering from channel mixing so that a wider receptive field does not require a dense convolution over every channel pair. Each residual block applies a 7 x 7 depthwise convolution before pointwise layers expand the channel dimension fourfold and project it back. Placing the spatial operation before expansion keeps the large kernel on the narrower representation, reserving most computation for dense channel transformations. A single LayerNorm and GELU simplify the block, while separate stride-two convolutions reduce resolution between stages. Normalization is also added at resolution transitions to stabilize this downsampling design. The architecture is developed through sequential modifications under a fixed 300-epoch AdamW training recipe, with approximately controlled FLOPs; reported accuracies in the smaller regime average three seeds. This procedure distinguishes gains from updated training from subsequent architectural gains, although intermediate models do not have identical computational costs.
cases.results: At 384 x 384 resolution with ImageNet-1K training, ConvNeXt-B reaches 85.1% top-1 accuracy versus 84.5% for Swin-B, while delivering 95.7 rather than 85.1 images per second on a V100 GPU. This comparison improves accuracy and measured inference throughput together, rather than merely reducing theoretical computation. The advantage is not restricted to classification: with ImageNet-22K pretraining and Cascade Mask R-CNN, ConvNeXt-B obtains 54.0 box AP and 46.9 mask AP on COCO, compared with 53.0 and 45.8 for Swin-B. The design trajectory also reveals that adopting Transformer conventions is not uniformly beneficial. Replacing ReLU with GELU alone leaves accuracy unchanged, kernels larger than 7 x 7 bring no further gains, and separate downsampling initially causes training to diverge unless normalization is added at resolution changes. These findings favor a tested combination of convolutional operations over any single borrowed component; they do not establish attention as unnecessary for multimodal interaction or structured-output tasks.
cases.notes: The abstract separates training-recipe gains from architecture gains and retains evidence of scaling and downstream utility. The roadmap's terminal 82.0% and Table 1's 82.1% are distinct reported results; neither is conflated here. Throughput values refer to V100 classification measurements. Sequential modifications support the tested design combination, not independent causal effects of every component. Multimodal and structured-output suitability remains a stated boundary, not an evaluated failure.

cases.abstract: High-quality novel-view synthesis must balance reconstruction fidelity against the cost of interactive rendering. We represent a static scene using anisotropic 3D Gaussians initialized from sparse structure-from-motion points, with learnable geometry, opacity, and spherical-harmonic appearance. Optimization alternates parameter updates with cloning, splitting, and pruning to allocate primitives where reconstruction needs them. A differentiable tile-based rasterizer sorts projected splats and blends them in approximate depth order, providing gradients without a fixed limit on contributing Gaussians. Evaluations cover 13 real scenes and synthetic bounded scenes. At 30,000 iterations, the real-scene dataset averages reach 134-154 frames per second on an A6000 GPU at their respective native resolutions, after approximately 27-42 minutes of training. Image quality is competitive with Mip-NeRF360 and improves over InstantNGP and Plenoxels, though Mip-NeRF360 retains higher PSNR on its own dataset. This rendering speed comes with substantially larger stored models than neural radiance-field baselines, and sparse view coverage or changes in blending order can still produce artifacts. The method thus enables interactive viewing through an explicit representation whose geometry and density are jointly adapted.
cases.methods: The Gaussian rasterizer makes explicit primitives useful for both optimization and interactive viewing by sharing visibility work across pixels. It divides the screen into 16 x 16 tiles, duplicates each projected Gaussian for the tiles it overlaps, and performs one GPU radix sort using tile identifiers and depth. Each tile then loads batches of splats into shared memory and blends them from front to back, stopping a pixel when opacity saturates. Because ordering is shared rather than recomputed per pixel, blending is approximate, particularly for large splats. During backpropagation, the same sorted lists are traversed in reverse and intermediate blending quantities are recovered from accumulated opacity, avoiding variable-length per-pixel storage. Crucially, every contributing splat can receive a gradient without a predetermined count limit. This design reduces sorting and storage overhead while preserving updates through scenes with varying depth complexity.
cases.results: On the Mip-NeRF360 dataset, 3D Gaussian splatting at 30,000 iterations yields SSIM of 0.815 versus the reference method's 0.792 and LPIPS of 0.214 versus 0.237, but PSNR is lower: 27.21 versus 27.69 dB. Competitive quality therefore does not imply superiority under every metric. Extending optimization from 7,000 to 30,000 iterations raises PSNR from 25.60 to 27.21 dB, while training time increases from 6 minutes 25 seconds to 41 minutes 33 seconds and rendering drops from 160 to 134 frames per second on an A6000 GPU. Stored model size also grows from 523 to 734 MB, compared with Mip-NeRF360's 8.6 MB. On Truck, limiting gradients to ten splats reduces 30,000-iteration PSNR from 24.81 to 13.84 dB and destabilizes optimization, supporting the decision to avoid a fixed gradient cap. These results expose the cost of interactive rendering: greater memory demand, with artifacts still possible in poorly observed regions or when large splats change blending order.
cases.notes: Real-scene rates and training times are dataset averages at differing native resolutions, not guarantees for every scene. Mip-NeRF360 quality values on its dataset are adopted from its publication. Its training cost comes from four A100 GPUs for 12 hours; no matched A6000 training-speed ratio is asserted. Memory figures used in the results describe stored optimized parameters, not peak training allocation. Successful random initialization on bounded synthetic scenes does not erase its adverse real-scene ablation.
